part_title: Multi-Region Entry and End-to-End Network Cost

scenes.title: Multi-Region traffic: DNS or anycast entry
scenes.visual_overview: Two alternatives branch from global users: Route 53 routing selects regional DNS answers; Global Accelerator uses static anycast IPs toward healthy regional endpoints.
visual_walkthrough: Compare left DNS options latency, weighted, failover and geographic policies, including TTL
compare right static anycast addresses, traffic dials and endpoint health
inspect Regions A and B and data readiness.
scenes.visual_example: A latency-sensitive global application needs stable entry IPs and rapid endpoint steering and considers Global Accelerator, while DNS policy may suffice for weighted rollout.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Select client entry based on DNS behavior versus anycast behavior, then separately verify regional health, capacity and data consistency.
scenes.narration: This slide compares two global entry strategies, not two services chained one after the other. Look at the left blue option. Amazon Route 53 makes a DNS answer decision. The rules can use latency, weights, failover health checks, or geographic logic. Because clients and resolvers cache DNS, time-to-live and caching behavior affect how quickly traffic shifts appear. On the right, AWS Global Accelerator provides stable anycast IP addresses for supported endpoint types. Traffic enters the AWS global network and is steered toward healthy regional endpoints according to health, configured traffic controls and applicable routing behavior. The colored branches below the options point to Region A and Region B, each with application and data resources that must already be ready to serve traffic. Neither option automatically copies state, migrates sessions or guarantees instant recovery. The lower middle callout distinguishes private backend networking, which might use inter-Region VPC peering, Transit Gateway peering or Cloud WAN, from the public client entry path. For architectural questions, choose whether DNS answers or static anycast IPs best meet requirements, then validate regional capacity, database replication and actual failover.

scenes.title: Estimate the whole network path
scenes.visual_overview: Five top cost dimensions include hourly resources, GB processed, cross-zone or inter-Region transfer, internet egress and operational resilience; comparisons cover endpoints and central NAT.
visual_walkthrough: compare gateway endpoint, interface endpoint and central egress panels
use bottom path-draw, volume estimate, regional price and resilience decision sequence.
scenes.visual_example: A central NAT design appears to save gateway hourly charges but adds TGW, NAT processing and cross-AZ transfer on realistic flow volumes.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Cost a complete bidirectional architecture with current regional prices, not one isolated hourly charge.
scenes.narration: Unlike the other diagrams, this is a cost accounting checklist. Along the top are five categories to collect for the complete network path: hourly resources, gigabytes processed, Availability Zone or Region transfer, internet egress where applicable, and operations and resilience. In the middle, consider the three design patterns separately. Gateway endpoints for supported S3 and DynamoDB traffic can keep eligible service traffic away from NAT processing, but service-specific data transfer rules still need checking. Interface endpoints have an hourly charge per endpoint Availability Zone as well as usage-based data processing charges, so compare realistic traffic. Centralized egress adds Transit Gateway and NAT Gateway charges, including processing, with possible cross-AZ considerations depending on placement. The warning bar notes that Transit Gateway itself has specific transfer charging behavior; surrounding resources may still introduce charges. At the bottom, the four-step sequence is a practical calculation method. Draw forward and return routes, estimate data volume for each component, apply current regional pricing, and compare resiliency and operational overhead. Do not claim one topology is cheaper until its actual path, direction and volume are modeled.
